title: Addressable Recall Compaction for Long Context-Window Control in AI Agents

images.desc:
Introduction


In recent years, the paradigm of Large Language Models (LLMs) (Masterman et al. 2024) has transitioned from passive text generation (Li et al. 2024) to active, autonomous agency. By embedding an LLM within an interactive execution loop, modern AI agents (Durante et al. 2024) can perceive environments, reason over objectives, and execute actions via external tools, APIs, or bash shells. At each discrete time step tt, the agent reads the cumulative historical transcript of the trajectory, synthesizes an internal monologue, and emits a structured action. The underlying runtime environment executes this action and appends the resulting observation back into the transcript, preparing the agent for the subsequent turn. Because contemporary autoregressive language models remain fundamentally stateless between independent API calls or inference passes, this monotonically growing transcript serves as the agent’s singular, monolithic working memory.


However, this architecture introduces a severe engineering and algorithmic bottleneck: the context-window limit (Tang et al. 2025). Every LLM is bounded by a strict maximum sequence length that it can process at once. Because the agentic trajectory at any given turn is a literal concatenation of all prior prompts, tool outputs, and environment responses, the transcript grows continuously and without bound as the agent keeps acting.


Once the cumulative transcript outgrows this maximum capacity, the system encounters an unrecoverable failure state: the LLM can no longer process the next step, effectively paralyzing the agent. For long-horizon planning (Erdogan et al. 2025), complex software engineering tasks, or open-ended web browsing, hitting this context wall is not a matter of if, but when rendering even modern ultra-large context windows insufficient.


Figure 1: Our Addressable Recall Compaction - ARC vs a standard agent context management.


Figure 2: Our Addressable Recall Compaction workflow.


To prevent this catastrophic overflow, contemporary agent frameworks rely on compaction or compression (Ichikawa et al. 2026): a suite of lossy transformation techniques designed to compress an over-long transcript into a truncated form that fits comfortably within context-window length. The current state-of-the-art methods generally fall into four paradigms:




• 

Naive Truncation (Wang et al. 2026): Dropping the oldest NN turns entirely, assuming older context is irrelevant.



• 

Hierarchical Summarization (Kang et al. 2026): Periodically prompting the LLM to condense historical turns into high-level textual summaries.



• 

State Folding (Fu et al. 2026): Mapping conversational histories into explicit, structured JSON or key-value state objects.



• 

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) (Park et al. 2023): Offloading historical context into an external vector database and retrieving relevant chunks via semantic similarity.





All four paradigms are fundamentally lossy: once history is pruned, paraphrased, or vectorized, exact recovery is no longer guaranteed. If the discarded content contains a critical needle such as a variable name, error string, or user constraint, the agent must either re-derive it at high cost or hallucinate a substitute, compounding errors over long trajectories.


We address this limitation by asking whether transcript compaction can remain strictly lossless while keeping the active prompt bounded. We introduce ARC (Addressable Recall Compaction) (Fig. 1), which decouples archival storage from in-context representation. ARC maintains (1) an append-only Addressable Store that preserves historical turns and tool outputs verbatim, and (2) a Bounded-Size Active View that replaces older content with explicit pointers into that store. With recall tools that resolve these pointers on demand, ARC preserves access to any historical needle without exceeding the active context budget.


Summary of Contributions




• 

We characterize how lossy compaction fails in long-horizon LLM agent trajectories.



• 

We present ARC, a lossless compaction framework based on addressable pointers and on-demand recall.



• 

We show that ARC prevents context-overflow failures and outperforms summarization- and RAG-based baselines on long-context, tool-heavy tasks.
